input:
This passage is intended to introduce the Prandtl number to second-year students who are encountering it for the first time, and its aim is to explain, in an accessible way, what this important dimensionless group actually means. The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, and although this definition can sound rather abstract at first sight, it expresses a very concrete comparison between two processes that take place inside a fluid.

Momentum diffusivity is, in essence, a measure of how rapidly a change in velocity is transmitted through a fluid: if the fluid at a wall is brought to rest, or set in motion, the influence of that change spreads progressively further into the surrounding fluid. Thermal diffusivity, on the other hand, measures how rapidly a disturbance in temperature spreads through the same fluid by conduction. By forming the ratio of the one quantity to the other, the Prandtl number compares the rates of these two spreading processes within a single material, and it is important to note that it is a property of the fluid and of its state, rather than a property of any particular flow in which the fluid happens to be involved.

Where the value of the Prandtl number is near 1, the implication is that momentum and heat spread through the fluid at broadly comparable rates. A velocity disturbance and a temperature disturbance starting at the same surface will penetrate similar distances in the same time, and the layer near the surface across which the velocity adjusts will have much the same thickness as the layer across which the temperature adjusts; at exactly 1, indeed, the two diffusivities are equal and neither process can be said to run ahead of the other. Where the value is large, by contrast, momentum spreads a great deal more rapidly than heat, and the velocity layer becomes much thicker than the temperature layer. At the other extreme, a value well below the near-1 range means that heat spreads faster than momentum, so that the temperature layer is the thicker of the two, a situation that is just as informative for the engineer who needs to interpret the behaviour of the fluid near a heated or cooled surface.
target:
The Prandtl number compares how fast momentum spreads through a fluid with how fast heat spreads through the same fluid. The passage is written for second-year students meeting the group for the first time.

The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how quickly a change in velocity at one place in a fluid is transmitted to the fluid around it; a shear applied at a wall is felt progressively further into the flow. Thermal diffusivity measures how quickly a temperature disturbance spreads through the same fluid by conduction. The Prandtl number divides the first rate by the second, so the number compares two spreading processes, and it is a property of the fluid and its state, not of the flow around it.

A value near 1 means the two rates are comparable: momentum and heat spread through the fluid at about the same speed. A disturbance in velocity and a disturbance in temperature imposed at the same surface reach similar distances into the fluid, and the layer near the surface in which the velocity is changing has about the same thickness as the layer in which the temperature is changing. At exactly 1 the two diffusivities are equal, and neither process runs ahead of the other.

A large value means momentum spreads much faster than heat. The velocity disturbance reaches deep into the fluid while the temperature disturbance is still confined close to the surface, so the velocity layer grows much thicker than the temperature layer. Heat then has to cross a comparatively thin region near the surface, and the temperature field responds to that thin region rather than to the whole moving fluid. A value well below the near-1 range reverses the comparison: heat spreads faster than momentum, the temperature layer outgrows the velocity layer, and a temperature disturbance is felt at distances the velocity disturbance has not yet reached. The Prandtl number therefore tells the reader, before any coefficient is calculated, whether momentum transfer or heat transfer sets the thicker layer at a surface.
